source.title: Analytic Study of Double Descent in Binary Classification: The Impact of Loss

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure labels and fractions appear flattened or inconsistent in the extraction.
record.tranche_reason: It analytically tests double-descent behavior in binary linear classifiers, using Gaussian data models and square-loss gradient descent rather than deep networks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own test-error curves for model-size and training-sample-size sweeps. Logistic-loss curves in Figures 1 and 4 are derived in cited companion work and are not treated as this paper's results. Training-error results are not recorded because the claim concerns test error.
record.test_reason: The paper derives sharp asymptotic test-error curves, checked by simulation, for converged square-loss GD in binary linear classifiers. It sweeps model size κ=p/n and training-set size. This is a different, analytic method on whether a non-deep model class shows a second descent past interpolation (V4) and whether more data can hurt (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors show analytically, with simulation checks at n=500 and 300 realizations, that converged square-loss GD on binary linear classification under Logistic and GM Gaussian models shows double descent with its cusp always at κ=1. The curve's shape beyond κ=1 and its global minimum depend on data model, feature-selection rule and SNR. Compared with logistic loss (results from the companion paper), the threshold and minimum also depend on the loss. For some model sizes, more training data increases test error.
record.recipe_differences: This is an analytic study of converged square-loss GD in binary linear classifiers with Gaussian features, not a deep-network size/epoch reproduction. It derives asymptotic risks and compares them with simulations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports changes with data model (Logistic or GM), feature-selection rule (linear or polynomial), SNR, loss function, and training-set size. It states that the overparameterized curve's shape depends on data and SNR, and that the cusp location depends on the loss.

fits_no_version.finding: The cusp location depends on the loss: always at κ=1 for square loss, but at a data-dependent κ⋆,LOG<1/2 for logistic loss. Logistic-loss curves come from the companion paper.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The location of the double-descent peak depends on the training algorithm (loss function), not only on model size relative to n.

record.problems: The settings are simplified binary linear classifiers with Gaussian features. Most curve values are available only in figures, without numeric uncertainty intervals. Simulations are reported for n=500 and averaged over 300 independent problem realizations. Some extracted figure labels and fractions are ambiguous.
record.rows_left_out: No additional test-error rows left out. Logistic-loss curves in Figures 1 and 4 are from cited companion work, not this paper's own results.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; only binary linear classifiers with Gaussian features.
No sweep over training time; GD is analyzed only at convergence.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across axes; κ is the only complexity measure.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple-peak analysis, no regularization tuning. SNR is varied but not tied to the presence of the peak.
There is no recasting by an effective number of parameters.
Only linear classifiers under Gaussian Logistic/GM data and two feature-selection rules. No other model classes.
One data model (Logistic), linear feature selection, theoretical curves only.

missing.what: Analytic result that test error converges to 1/2 (chance) as κ→1 from either side, for both data models, irrespective of r and s.
Statement that the global minimum is in the overparameterized regime for GM data at high enough SNR, but at κ<1 for Logistic data with polynomial features.
Statement that the interpolation threshold shifts right as n grows. The global minimum is at p=d for all n, with lower error for larger n.
missing.locator: Section 4.3 'On the size of the training set'; Figure 5

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. Tranche could arguably be T3 (new setting); kept at T2 because it is an analytic test of the same model-size question. Figure-only evidence; no uncertainty reported for the curves. The logistic-loss comparison (Figs 1, 4) is correctly excluded from rows as companion-paper results.

versions.untested_parts: The size sweep is over binary linear classifiers, not deep networks.
No sweep over training epochs; GD is analyzed at convergence.
The reported example is for a particular linear feature-selection model, data model, and model size; it does not establish the effect for all settings.
The study covers binary linear classification with two Gaussian-feature data models, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs, and sample-size axes.
SNR is varied, but label-noise or variance as a cause of the peak, multiple descent peaks, and optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
The study does not recast the curve using an effective number of parameters.

rows.baseline: At n=15 d, test error is lowest among the compared sample sizes; numerical value not stated.
rows.value: At n=35 d, test error is largest among the compared sample sizes; numerical value not stated.
rows.locator: Figure 5; Section 4.3, 'On the size of the training set'
rows.note: The authors explicitly report that at this model size more training examples can hurt. The paper's extracted fractions are ambiguous; Figure 5 also labels the curves using ζ.
rows.check: Training sizes are mis-extracted: '15 d' and '35 d' are n=(1/5)d and n=(3/5)d, the three curves being 1/5, 2/5 and 3/5 d (ζ=5, 5/2, 5/3). Analytic curves only, no simulation; model size is p≈0.5d.

relationships.reason: Test error peaks at the interpolation threshold κ=1 (analytically →1/2, Remark 2) and descends again beyond it, in all plots (R1–R12).
relationships.display_finding: Test error peaked at κ=1, analytically approaching 1/2, and declined beyond the threshold in every plotted setting.
